Lucas Gernler
loo'kas gern'ler
n. (Lucas Gernler, 1625–1675, antistes of Basel and co-author of the Helvetic Consensus)
Greek Loukas, of Lucania; Germanic Gernler, a Swiss surname.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lucas Gernler was professor of theology and then antistes — chief pastor — of the church at Basel, and with Heidegger of Zurich and Francis Turretin of Geneva he was one of the three men chiefly responsible for the Formula Consensus Helvetica. His part was to carry Basel, which had the most independent of the Swiss theological faculties and the most to lose from a tight subscription, and he did it. He died the year the Formula was adopted. The dictionary records him as the man who did the persuading. A confession has an author and it also has the men who go from city to city getting magistrates and faculties to sign, and the second labour is usually the harder. Gernler spent the last years of a short life travelling between Swiss cantons arguing that a softening in France was a danger in Switzerland, which is the sort of argument nobody thanks a man for making.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines antistes as a chief priest or presiding minister, and subscribe as to attest by writing one's name beneath.

expand to see more

AN'TISTES, n. A chief or presiding minister; among the Swiss Reformed, the chief pastor of a city church.

SUBSCRI'BE, v.t. To attest by writing the name beneath; to assent to.

FAC'ULTY, n. The body of professors or instructors in a university or one of its departments.

CAN'TON, n. A small division of territory, as the cantons of Switzerland.

Modern Corruption

He carried Basel for the Helvetic Consensus and died the year it was adopted.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a doctrinal danger abroad is somebody else's business. Basel had no quarrel with Saumur and no immediate trouble of its own; Gernler's argument was that an error allowed anywhere in the Reformed communion will arrive everywhere in a generation, and the century that followed proved him right in the worst way.

The principle to recover is that contending for the faith is a corporate duty, and that churches owe one another plain speech. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The pattern is to be held and not improvised: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13). And the model of a church speaking with one voice is the Jerusalem letter: “It seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord” (Act 15:25).

Greek epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; Greek homothumadon (G3661), with one accord.

Usage

"“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jud 1:3) — Basel persuaded to subscribe in 1675."

"“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — three men, three cities, one formula."

"“being assembled with one accord” (Act 15:25) — a short life spent travelling between cantons."
